summary: Describes how to prepare internationalized domain name labels so that input and comparison work sensibly for users everywhere. It is a profile of stringprep and is part of the set of protocols for internationalizing DNS. It was replaced by RFC 5891.

eli5.summary: Different ways of typing the same name should still find the same website. Nameprep cleans names up so look-alike spellings match. It was later replaced by RFC 5891.

questions: what does nameprep do in idna
subtitle: The rulebook for cleaning up internationalized domain name labels so look-alike inputs compare as equal.

tldr.problem: Users all over the world type internationalized domain names in different but equivalent ways, so names need preparing before they are compared or looked up.
tldr.mechanism: Nameprep is a profile of stringprep: it works on Unicode 3.2, maps characters with two tables, applies Unicode normalization form KC, rejects characters from a list of prohibited tables and checks bidirectional strings.
tldr.outcome: Nameprep is used by IDNA for each label of a domain name. It has been obsoleted by RFC 5891.

today: RFC 3491 is obsoleted by RFC 5891. It was a Proposed Standard published in March 2003.

sections.title: What Nameprep Is For
sections.content:
This document specifies processing rules that let users enter internationalized domain names (IDNs) into applications and have the best chance of getting the content of the strings right. It is a profile of stringprep (RFC 3454) and is meant only for internationalized domain names, not for arbitrary text. It SHOULD NOT be used for free text.

Nameprep is used by the IDNA protocol (RFC 3490). IDNA calls it once for each label in a domain name, not for the whole name. Implementations of Nameprep MUST fully implement stringprep.
sections.eli5: Nameprep is a cleaning step for one piece of a web address at a time, like tidying each word in a sentence. It is only for web names, not for ordinary writing.

sections.title: The Profile in Five Choices
sections.content:
Stringprep requires every profile to state its choices. For nameprep they are:

  • Character repertoire: Unicode 3.2, as defined in stringprep Appendix A.
  • Mapping: tables B.1 and B.2 from stringprep.
  • Normalization: Unicode normalization form KC.
  • Prohibited output: tables C.1.2, C.2.2, C.3, C.4, C.5, C.6, C.7, C.8 and C.9.
  • Bidirectional characters: checked as described in section 6 of stringprep.

The RFC adds an important note: this profile MUST be used with IDNA, because IDNA has additional prohibitions that are checked outside of the profile.
sections.eli5: Nameprep makes five choices: which letters are allowed, how to swap similar ones, how to write them in one standard way, which are banned, and how to handle right-to-left writing.

sections.title: Unassigned Code Points
sections.content: If the IDNA processing says a list of unassigned code points should be used, the system uses table A.1 from stringprep as that list. Unassigned code points are characters that Unicode 3.2 has not given a meaning to.
sections.eli5: Some spots in the big list of letters are still empty. Nameprep has a list of those empty spots so they can be handled properly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unicode and ISO/IEC 10646 have many characters that look alike. Stringprep does nothing to map similar-looking characters together or to prohibit characters because they look like others, because that is impossible without context such as the fonts in use.

Because security on the Internet partly relies on the DNS, a change to DNS characteristics can change the security of much of the Internet. It would be a compromise if a user entering one internationalized name could reach different servers because of different interpretations of it. The RFC also warns that this document vastly increases the number of characters available in domain names, so programs that treat special characters in connection with domain names may be vulnerable to attack.
sections.eli5: Some letters from different alphabets look the same, and nameprep cannot tell them apart by sight. Programs need to be careful about the many new letters now allowed in names.
